entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
York Minster is the largest Gothic cathedral in Northern Europe and one of the finest examples of Gothic architecture in the world, built in the heart of York, England, between 1220 and 1472 CE. Seat of the Archbishop of York, the second-highest office in the Church of England after Canterbury, it contains the largest collection of medieval stained glass in England including the Great East Window — the world's largest expanse of medieval stained glass.

The site has been a place of Christian worship since 627 CE when King Edwin of Northumbria was baptized by Bishop Paulinus in a small wooden church that was the first York Minster. The current Gothic building, incorporating earlier Roman, Saxon, and Norman remains in its foundations, took 252 years to complete in stages — the chapter house (1270s), nave (1291-1360), towers, and finally the central tower (1471). The Gothic construction incorporated innovative engineering: the central tower rebuilt in 1470s used a novel 'inverted arch' support system still visible in the undercroft.

York Minster houses extraordinary medieval treasures: the Great West Window (1338) known as the 'Heart of Yorkshire' for its elegant tracery; Five Sisters Window (1250) the oldest complete window in England; and the Great East Window (1405-1408) covering 18 square meters depicting the beginning and end of all things. A devastating 1984 fire caused by lightning destroyed the south transept roof, prompting a £2.25 million restoration that completed in 1988.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: York Minster's 252-year Gothic construction created the largest collection of medieval stained glass in England, establishing the seat of the Archbishop of York and the religious heart of northern England for 1,400 years.
